notes:
Here are my verse-by-verse notes on Jeremiah 6, drawn from the sources I was able to access. Where I could not find material on specific traditions, I have noted that.

---

## Jeremiah 6 – Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — "Run for cover, O sons of Benjamin; flee from Jerusalem…"

Jerusalem, though the capital of Judah, lay geographically within the territory of Benjamin (the boundary between Judah and Benjamin ran through the Valley of Hinnom). Jeremiah, himself a Benjaminite from Anathoth, addresses his own tribesmen. The irony is sharp: the tribe that housed the sanctuary and was "the beloved of the Lord" (Deut 33:12) is now told to flee from the holy city because God Himself is bringing disaster. (Ellicott)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm

Tekoa was about 12 miles south of Jerusalem, in the hill country of Judah, the birthplace of Amos. The Hebrew presents a word-play: *tiq‘û* ("blow") sounds like *Təqôa‘*. Such paronomasia is a favourite prophetic device (cf. Micah 1:10–16). (Pulpit Commentary)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm

Beth-haccerem ("house of the vineyard") lay on an eminence between Jerusalem and Tekoa. Jerome identified it with the Frank Mountain (Jebel Fureidis), an ideal location for a signal-fire visible for miles. The signal (*masso’at*) was a fire-signal, such as those used in ancient Mesopotamian military communication and mentioned in the Lachish Letters. (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

"Disaster looms from the north" — literally "is bending over" or looking down on its prey. The same verb is used of righteousness "looking down from heaven" in Psalm 85:11. The invader would come from the north (Babylon), following the Euphrates and then turning south, since the Arabian desert lay east of Palestine. (Ellicott; Bible.org)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

---

### v. 2 — "Though she is beautiful and delicate, I will destroy the Daughter of Zion."

This verse is textually difficult. The traditional rendering (KJV, NKJV) takes it as God likening Zion to a lovely and delicate woman — beautiful but utterly defenceless before an invading army. (Enduring Word)
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

However, some scholars (and the NJB) point out that the Hebrew word translated "comely" (*nāweh*) can also mean "pasture" or "habitation" (as in Exod 15:13; Isa 65:10). They render it: "I have likened the daughter of Zion to a fair pasturage" — which sets up the shepherd/flock imagery of the next verse. The Pulpit Commentary finds the text possibly corrupted, its original surviving only in fragments. (Ellicott; Pulpit Commentary)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm

---

### v. 3 — "Shepherds and their flocks will come against her…"

"Shepherds" here refers to the commanders of the invading armies, and their "flocks" are their soldiers. The image is drawn from nomadic tribes sweeping onto rich pasture-land and devouring everything. "Each tending his own portion" (literally, "each at his hand") means every commander will plunder at will in the area assigned to him. (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

---

### vv. 4–5 — "Prepare for battle… let us attack at noon… by night…"

The verb "prepare" (literally "sanctify" or "consecrate," *qaddəšû*) suggests the religious rituals that accompanied ancient warfare — sacrifices and divinations before battle (cf. Deut 20:1–3 for Israel; Ezek 21:20–22 for the Chaldeans). The invaders are dramatically portrayed urging one another on. (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

"Woe to us, for the daylight is fading" — these are the words of the invading soldiers, impatient because the day is ending. They had hoped to attack at noon (when defenders might be resting in the heat), but the march took too long. Now they urge a night assault instead — so fierce is their eagerness that they will not even wait for dawn. (Ellicott; Bible.org)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

**Traditional reading across traditions:** These verses present the invaders as agents of God's judgment. The urgency and relentlessness of the attack reflect divine determination. The fact that they attack at unusual times (noon and night) underscores the severity of the coming judgment. (Enduring Word; Bible.org)

---

### v. 6 — "Cut down the trees and raise a siege ramp against Jerusalem…"

The LORD of Hosts Himself commands the siege. Cutting down trees was standard practice for siege-works: timber was used for building mounds, battering rams, and siege engines (see Assyrian bas-reliefs). Deuteronomy 20:19–20 regulated this for Israel, forbidding the destruction of fruit trees. (Ellicott)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm

"Raise a siege ramp" (literally "pour a mound") — baskets of earth were emptied to build a ramp reaching to the level of the city wall, enabling the attackers to deploy battering rams effectively. (Pulpit Commentary)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm

"This city must be punished" — the Hebrew verb *pāqad* (to visit) can mean either blessing or cursing; here it is visitation for judgment. The reason: "nothing but oppression in her midst." (Bible.org)
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

**Reformed perspective (Ligonier):** God is described as the one who ordered the siege ramps. He is sovereign over the pagan armies, using them as His instruments, which is "His right as the sovereign of the world." This reflects the Reformed emphasis on God's absolute sovereignty even over evil nations as instruments of His holy wrath. (Ligonier)
https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-and-city

---

### v. 7 — "As a well gushes its water, so she pours out her evil."

Evil in Jerusalem was not occasional but constant and natural to the city — like a well or cistern that continuously yields fresh (cool) water. The Pulpit Commentary renders it: "as a cistern keepeth fresh (literally, cool) her waters, so she keepeth fresh her wickedness." Wickedness was ingrained, passing into act by a law of nature. (Pulpit Commentary)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm

"Violence and destruction resound in her" — the Hebrew words denote injustice (*ḥāmās*) and violent devastation (*šōd*). "Sickness and wounds" are metaphors for the moral and spiritual condition of the nation, constantly before God's face. (Bible.org; Ellicott)
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm

---

### v. 8 — "Be forewarned, O Jerusalem, or I will turn away from you…"

"Be forewarned" (or "be corrected," "let yourself be chastened") — this is an invitation. Even within the pronouncement of judgment, God offers the opportunity to receive correction and avoid the threatened calamity. The verb is a *Niphal* tolerative: "let yourself accept discipline." (Pulpit Commentary; Enduring Word)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

"Lest My soul depart from you" — literally, "lest my soul be torn from you." This is the worst possible outcome: alienation from God. The language parallels the marriage metaphor running through Jeremiah's prophecies. (Pulpit Commentary; Bible.org)

---

### v. 9 — "Glean the remnant of Israel as thoroughly as a vine."

The image is of a grape-gatherer who goes over the vine again and again, hand reaching into every branch, leaving nothing behind. Israel had already been reduced to a "remnant" (the northern ten tribes exiled in 722 BC, only Judah remaining). Now even Judah would be gleaned with thorough desolation. Yet believers might recall that a few grapes were always left at the edges after harvest (Isa 17:6; cf. Jer 4:27; 5:10, 18 — God promises not to make a full end). (Pulpit Commentary; Bible.org)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

---

### v. 10 — "To whom can I give this warning? Who will listen?"

Jeremiah speaks in his own voice, expressing the prophet's frustration. "Their ears are closed" — literally "their ear is uncircumcised," a unique phrase in the OT (the only mention of an uncircumcised ear; elsewhere the heart or lips are said to be uncircumcised). The metaphor means their hearing organ is covered with a "foreskin," preventing God's word from entering. Stephen quoted this image in Acts 7:51. (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

"The word of the LORD has become offensive to them; they find no pleasure in it." God's word, which was meant to be a delight (Ps 19:7–10), had become an object of scorn. (Bible.org; Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 11–12 — "I am full of the LORD's wrath… Pour it out…"

The prophet is filled to bursting with the divine fury and can no longer hold it in. The imperative "Pour it out!" is either God commanding Jeremiah or Jeremiah's higher prophetic self addressing his human self. (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott)

Judgment will fall on every segment of society: children playing in the streets, young men in their social gatherings, husband and wife, the aged and the very elderly — none are spared. Houses, fields, and even wives will be transferred to others (cf. Deut 28:30). Wives are here regarded as property, in the legal sense of the ancient world. (Ellicott; Bible.org)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

---

### v. 13 — "From the least of them to the greatest, all are greedy for gain; from prophet to priest, all practice deceit."

The corruption is universal — both in social standing ("least to greatest") and in spiritual office ("prophet to priest"). The Hebrew for "greedy for gain" uses the verb and noun of the same root (*bṣ‘*), meaning "to tear away" unjust gain. (Ellicott; Bible.org)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

**Traditional reading (all traditions):** The two classes that should have checked the evil — prophets and priests — were foremost in promoting it. This is a recurring theme through Jeremiah (cf. 5:31; 8:10).

---

### v. 14 — "They dress the wound of My people with very little care, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace at all."

This is one of the most cited verses in Jeremiah. The false prophets and priests acted like physicians who treat a fatal wound as though it were a minor scratch — "as men use to cure the slight hurts of their children by blowing on them only, or stroking them over" (Trapp, cited by Enduring Word). The word "slightly" (or "superficially," "as a thing of nought") underscores their negligence. (Enduring Word; Ellicott)
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm

**John Piper (Baptist/Reformed):** Applied this verse to the modern "peacetime mentality" that tells people to "pad your life" while spiritual warfare rages. He warns that "until we feel the desperation of a bombing raid," we will not pray rightly. (DesiringGod)
https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-comfortable-christians-go-prayerless

**Charles Spurgeon (Baptist):** In his sermon "A Blast of the Trumpet Against False Peace," identified several ways people receive false peace: through entertainment and distraction, by denying God's existence, by ignorance of the things of God, or by intending to do better later. (Cited in Enduring Word)
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

**G. Campbell Morgan:** Suggested false prophets say "peace, peace" in multiple ways — by silence (refusing to address evil), by speaking of evil as merely "the underside of good," or by denying evil exists at all. (Cited in Enduring Word)

---

### v. 15 — "Are they ashamed…? No, they have no shame at all; they do not even know how to blush."

The conscience of the nation was so seared that the normal human response to shameful behaviour — blushing — had been lost. Ellicott notes this is "the most hopeless of all states." The Hebrew word-order suggests they had already been brought to shame by their abominations, yet they felt no inward shame at all. "Therefore they shall fall among the fallen" — what happened to other rebels will happen to them (possibly alluding to the fall of the northern kingdom in 722 BC). (Ellicott; Bible.org)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

---

### v. 16 — "Stand at the crossroads and look. Ask for the ancient paths: 'Where is the good way?' Then walk in it, and you will find rest for your souls."

This is the heart of Jeremiah 6 and one of the most beloved verses in the book. God gives five imperatives: stand, see, ask, walk, and find. The image is of a traveller at a crossroads, uncertain which path to take, who stops to inquire from those who know the way. (Pulpit Commentary; Enduring Word)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

"The old paths" — literally "the eternal paths" (going beyond mere antiquity). These are the tried-and-true ways of Mosaic tradition and the covenant — the way of repentance, reconciliation, fear and love of God. Ellicott notes the path metaphor was common in wisdom literature (cf. Ps 119:105; Prov 6:23). (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm

"Rest for your souls" — Jesus quoted this in Matthew 11:29: "Take My yoke upon you and learn from Me… and you will find rest for your souls." His teachings fulfil and surpass the ancient paths. (Bible.org; Enduring Word)
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

"But they said, 'We will not walk in it!'" — The tragedy: God offered wisdom, but His people explicitly refused.

**John Piper (Baptist/Reformed):** Cited this verse to warn against chronological snobbery: "People think new ideas are better than old ideas. That's not necessarily the case." (DesiringGod)
https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/four-mistakes-i-hope-you-dont-make

---

### v. 17 — "I appointed watchmen over you… 'Listen for the sound of the ram's horn.' But they answered, 'We will not listen!'"

The "watchmen" are the prophets (cf. Isa 52:8; 56:10; Ezek 3:17; Hab 2:1). Standing on their high watch-tower, they scrutinise the horizon for the first sign of danger and blow the trumpet of alarm. But the people's response was defiant refusal. God "kept raising up" watchmen (frequentative perfect), showing His persistent grace. (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm

---

### vv. 18–19 — "Therefore hear, O nations… I am bringing disaster on this people, the fruit of their own schemes."

With remonstrance useless, God summons the Gentile nations and the earth itself as witnesses to the judgment. The "congregation" (Hebrew *‘ēdâ*) probably refers to the assembled nations, not Israel — an unusual usage. The disaster is "the fruit of their thoughts" — they are reaping what they have sown, a doctrine found in both Testaments (Isa 3:10; Jas 1:15). (Pulpit Commentary; Bible.org)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

---

### v. 20 — "What use to Me is frankincense from Sheba or sweet cane from a distant land?"

Frankincense from Sheba (south-west Arabia) and sweet cane (calamus, from India) were expensive ingredients used in temple incense and anointing oil (Exod 30:23, 34). God rejects even costly worship when the worshipper's heart is disobedient. The same theme runs through Isa 1:11–14; Hos 6:6; Amos 5:21–23; Mic 6:6–8. It was not the sacrificial system God instituted that He rejected, but the attitude and disobedience of the worshippers. (Ellicott; Bible.org)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

**All Protestant traditions agree:** Religious ceremony cannot cover rebellion against God's word. This is a foundational principle for the Reformation's emphasis on faith and obedience over mere ritual.

---

### v. 21 — "I will lay stumbling blocks before this people; fathers and sons alike will be staggered."

The "stumbling blocks" are the Babylonians — instruments of God's judgment. Where God's people should have been walking the "ancient path" leading to life, God Himself places obstacles on their self-chosen path. Fathers and sons, neighbours and friends — all relationships — will perish together. This reverses the blessing of Isaiah 54:15 for the regenerate Israel of the future. (Pulpit Commentary; Bible.org)
https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/6.htm

**Christian reading (Enduring Word):** This naturally connects with the NT idea that Messiah is the cornerstone; those who reject Him stumble over it (1 Pet 2:7). (Enduring Word)

---

### vv. 22–23 — "An army is coming from the land of the north… cruel and merciless…"

The description matches the Babylonians (and possibly Scythian elements). Key features:
- They come "from the farthest parts of the earth" — Mesopotamia.
- Armed with bow and javelin — the distinctive weapons of the Chaldeans (cf. Jer 5:16).
- "Cruel and have no mercy" — the Babylonians' ferocity was proverbial: prisoners impaled, flayed alive, or burnt (cf. Jer 29:22; Dan 3:11). Yet Rawlinson notes the Assyrians were not *naturally* hard-hearted; they sometimes spared those who surrendered. (Ellicott)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
- "Their voice roars like the sea" — the horrid roar of advancing hosts struck terror (cf. Isa 5:30; 17:12–13).
- "They ride upon horses" — cavalry was a novelty to Israelites accustomed to war-chariots. (Ellicott)

---

### vv. 24–26 — "We have heard the report; our hands hang limp…"

Jeremiah identifies himself with his people, dramatising the terror: limp hands (from fear), anguish like a woman in labour (cf. Jer 4:31), fear of even venturing outside the city walls. "Fear is on every side" — Hebrew *māgôr missābîb*, one of Jeremiah's characteristic phrases (cf. 20:3, 10; 46:5; 49:29). It became a watchword, even a name Jeremiah gave to Pashhur (Jer 20:3). (Ellicott; Bible.org)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6

"Dress in sackcloth and roll in ashes… mourn as for an only son." Rolling in ashes (not just sprinkling them on the head) indicated the most utter wretchedness. The "mourning for an only son" was the most bitter grief imaginable. The Septuagint renders it "mourning for a beloved one." Some scholars see a possible allusion to the rites for the Phoenician god Adonis (Thammuz, cf. Ezek 8:14), but the ordinary explanation — that it represents the deepest human grief — is "perfectly tenable and more obvious." (Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott)

---

### vv. 27–30 — "I have appointed you to examine My people like ore…"

God addresses Jeremiah directly. The prophet's task is compared to a metal refiner. The imagery:
- **Jeremiah is the assayer/tester** — set among the people to assess their spiritual condition. The Hebrew for "fortress" (*mibṣār*) is difficult; some revocalise it as "assessor" (RSV), making it a gloss on "assayer." (Enduring Word; Bible.org)
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/
https://bible.org/seriespage/jeremiah-6
- **The people are base metals** (bronze and iron) — hard and impure, not soft like silver or gold that could be refined. They are "stubborn rebels" (literally "rebels of rebels," a Hebrew superlative).
- **The bellows and fire** represent the prophetic word and divine judgment — intensely hot, meant to purify.
- **Lead** was used as a flux in smelting silver ore, to draw out impurities. Even the lead was consumed, yet "the wicked are not purged" — the refining was in vain.

The tragic conclusion: "They are called rejected silver, because the LORD has rejected them." The Hebrew uses the same root for "rejected" (adjective) and "has rejected" (verb), creating a striking word-play: *kesep nim’ās* … *mā’as YHWH*. What claimed to be precious silver turned out to be worthless dross. (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/jeremiah/6.htm
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/

**Derek Kidner** (cited in Enduring Word): "This picture of the prophet's words as a refiner's fire makes its point … it emerges that the people of Judah are not, so to speak, precious metal marred by some impurities, but base metal from which nothing of worth can be extracted."

---

## Denominational Distinctives

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The Ligonier devotional emphasises God's sovereignty in judgment: God Himself "ordered the building of siege ramps" and brought the pagan armies. The people trusted in the temple's physical presence, but "the Lord's holy wrath would judge His impenitent people." This reflects the Reformed stress on divine sovereignty, covenant, and the danger of presumption. (Ligonier)
https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/ark-and-city

### Baptist
Charles Spurgeon applied "Peace, peace, when there is no peace" to the danger of false assurance. John Piper (DesiringGod) has used v. 14 to warn against a "peacetime mentality" that ignores spiritual warfare, and v. 16 to warn against rejecting ancient wisdom simply because it is old. These applications reflect Baptist emphases on personal conversion, genuine faith, and the authority of Scripture. No distinctively Baptist *doctrinal* divergence on the passage emerged from the sources consulted.
https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-comfortable-christians-go-prayerless
https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/four-mistakes-i-hope-you-dont-make

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
David Guzik (Enduring Word / Calvary Chapel) provides thorough verse-by-verse exposition. His approach is broadly evangelical/charismatic with no distinctively Pentecostal doctrinal divergence on this text. He does warn about "self-appointed watchmen" in the modern internet age, noting a difference "between those who are set by God and those who are self-appointed." (Enduring Word)
https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-6/
